**[Section 6: Duration of Status and Extensions]{.underline}**

**6.1 Initial Period of Stay and Extensions**

H-1B status is initially approved for a period of up to three years, as provided in 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(9)(iii)(A)(1). The actual period of approved status may be shorter than three years depending on the validity period of the employer\'s LCA, the terms of the employment, or other case-specific considerations, but the three-year period represents the maximum initial approval.

Extensions of H-1B status may be granted in increments of up to three additional years per extension. Under INA § 214(g)(4), however, the total cumulative period of stay in H-1B status is limited to a maximum of six years. Once a beneficiary has been in H-1B status for a total of six years --- whether with one employer or multiple employers --- the beneficiary must generally depart the United States and remain abroad for at least one full year before becoming eligible for a new H-1B petition. During this one-year absence, any time spent in the United States in other nonimmigrant statuses does not count toward the one-year requirement; the beneficiary must be physically outside the United States.

**6.2 AC21 Extensions Beyond Six Years**

The six-year maximum period of stay in H-1B status, while seemingly rigid, is subject to two critically important statutory exceptions created by the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act of 2000 (\"AC21\"). These exceptions are among the most consequential provisions in employment-based immigration law and are essential tools for long-term workforce retention planning.

**AC21 § 104(c) --- One-Year Extensions Based on Approved I-140 and Visa Unavailability.** Under Section 104(c) of AC21, an H-1B worker who is the beneficiary of an approved I-140 immigrant visa petition may obtain one-year extensions of H-1B status beyond the six-year maximum if the beneficiary is unable to file an application for adjustment of status to permanent residence due to the unavailability of an immigrant visa number. This provision is designed to address the lengthy per-country backlogs in the employment-based immigrant visa categories, particularly the EB-2 and EB-3 categories for nationals of India and China. Under current visa bulletin projections, Indian nationals in the EB-2 category may face wait times of ten years or more from the priority date to visa number availability. Without the AC21 § 104(c) extension mechanism, these beneficiaries would be forced to leave the United States after six years despite having an approved immigrant petition and would be unable to continue employment in the United States during the pendency of their green card process. AC21 § 104(c) extensions may be obtained indefinitely --- in successive one-year increments --- until the beneficiary\'s priority date becomes current and the beneficiary is able to file for adjustment of status or consular process for an immigrant visa.

**AC21 § 106(a) --- Three-Year Extensions Based on Lengthy Adjudication.** Under Section 106(a) of AC21, an H-1B worker may obtain extensions of H-1B status in three-year increments beyond the six-year maximum if the employer has filed a PERM labor certification application or an I-140 immigrant visa petition on the beneficiary\'s behalf at least 365 days before the end of the beneficiary\'s six-year H-1B period and the application or petition remains pending or has been approved. This provision addresses situations where the green card process --- particularly the often-lengthy PERM labor certification stage --- has been initiated in a timely manner but has not been completed before the H-1B six-year clock expires. The 365-day filing threshold is a strict deadline: if the PERM or I-140 is filed fewer than 365 days before the end of the H-1B period, the beneficiary does not qualify for a § 106(a) extension. Early initiation of the PERM labor certification process is therefore essential to preserving AC21 § 106(a) eligibility.

Both AC21 § 104(c) and § 106(a) extensions are available regardless of the employer\'s cap-exempt or cap-subject status, and they apply to beneficiaries of all nationalities, though they are most frequently utilized by Indian and Chinese nationals facing the most significant per-country visa backlogs.

**Practical Note for Aethon.** Given that several of Aethon\'s planned 35 hires are likely to be Indian nationals --- including, for example, Rajeev Malhotra --- AC21 extensions are critically important for Aethon\'s long-term workforce planning. Indian nationals in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories face the longest backlogs in the employment-based immigration system, and it is virtually certain that any Indian national hired by Aethon in H-1B status will require AC21 extensions to remain employed beyond the initial six-year H-1B period. Counsel strongly recommends that Aethon initiate the PERM labor certification process for each H-1B employee as early as practicable --- ideally within the first year of H-1B employment --- to ensure that the 365-day threshold for AC21 § 106(a) eligibility is met well before the H-1B six-year expiration date. Early PERM initiation also provides a buffer for processing delays and potential audit responses that may extend the PERM adjudication timeline. The firm will advise on specific PERM filing timelines for each candidate as part of the overall immigration strategy.

**[Section 7: H-1B Portability (Change of Employer)]{.underline}**

**7.1 AC21 § 105 Portability**

One of the most significant practical features of the H-1B classification is the portability provision established by AC21 § 105, codified at INA § 214(n). Under this provision, an H-1B nonimmigrant worker may begin employment with a new employer upon the filing of a non-frivolous H-1B petition by the new employer, without waiting for USCIS to approve the petition. This mechanism --- commonly referred to as \"H-1B portability\" or \"H-1B transfer\" --- dramatically reduces the disruption and delay associated with changing employers and provides meaningful labor market mobility for H-1B workers.

To invoke H-1B portability, the following conditions must be met:

> **(1)** The beneficiary must be in valid H-1B nonimmigrant status at the time the new employer files the change-of-employer petition;
>
> **(2)** The beneficiary must have been lawfully admitted to the United States;
>
> **(3)** The new employer must file a non-frivolous H-1B petition on the beneficiary\'s behalf before the beneficiary\'s current H-1B status expires; and
>
> **(4)** The beneficiary must not have been employed without authorization in the United States since the date of the beneficiary\'s last lawful admission.

Once a change-of-employer petition is filed and a receipt notice is issued by USCIS, the beneficiary may immediately commence employment with the new petitioning employer. The beneficiary may continue working for the new employer while the petition is pending, even if the prior employer\'s H-1B petition is subsequently revoked or the prior employment is terminated.

This provision is directly relevant to Aethon\'s hiring strategy. If Aethon seeks to recruit engineers or scientists who are currently employed by other companies in H-1B status, the change-of-employer petition filed by Aethon will be cap-exempt --- because the beneficiary was already counted against the cap in a prior fiscal year --- and the candidate may begin work at Aethon upon filing. The H-1B modernization rule published in January 2024 codified and clarified several aspects of the portability framework, confirming that the beneficiary may begin work with the new employer upon receipt of the filing by USCIS and further specifying the documentation requirements for portability petitions.

**7.2 Concurrent Employment**

An H-1B worker may also work concurrently for more than one employer, provided that each employer files a separate H-1B petition for the beneficiary. The concurrent employment petition filed by the second (or subsequent) employer is cap-exempt if the beneficiary is already in valid H-1B status by virtue of the primary employer\'s petition, as the beneficiary has already been counted against the cap. Each employer must independently satisfy all H-1B requirements, including obtaining a certified LCA and establishing a valid employer-employee relationship. The practical relevance of concurrent employment petitions is limited for Aethon\'s current hiring plans, as the company does not anticipate part-time or concurrent arrangements for its planned positions. This provision is included here for completeness and may become relevant in future scenarios involving consulting or advisory arrangements.

**[Section 9: H-1B Eligibility Checklist]{.underline}**

The following pre-screening checklist is provided for use by Brightfield & Novak LLP attorneys and authorized Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc. HR personnel in evaluating whether a particular position and candidate may be suitable for H-1B sponsorship. This checklist is a preliminary screening tool only and does not substitute for a full legal assessment by qualified immigration counsel.

**Position Requirements:**

> • \[ \] Does the position require, at minimum, a bachelor\'s degree or higher in a specific specialty directly related to the job duties?
>
> • \[ \] Can the employer demonstrate that the position meets at least one of the four specialty occupation criteria under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(ii)?
>
> • \[ \] Has a detailed position description been prepared specifying the specialized duties, technical competencies, and educational requirements of the role?
>
> • \[ \] If the position involves work at a third-party worksite, has supporting documentation (contracts, itineraries, supervisory plans) been prepared?

**Beneficiary Qualifications:**

> • \[ \] Does the candidate hold a U.S. bachelor\'s degree or foreign equivalent in the required field or a directly related specialty?
>
> • \[ \] If the candidate\'s degree is from a foreign institution, has a credential evaluation been obtained or has one been scheduled with an accredited evaluation service?
>
> • \[ \] If relying on experience equivalency rather than a four-year degree, does the candidate have sufficient progressively responsible experience (three years of experience per year of missing education under the three-for-one rule)?
>
> • \[ \] Does the candidate require any state-specific professional license for the position? If so, does the candidate hold or is the candidate eligible for the required license?

**Employer Compliance:**

> • \[ \] Has the employer determined the applicable prevailing wage level for the position and geographic area (Austin, TX MSA or other applicable area)?
>
> • \[ \] Is the proposed salary at or above the higher of the actual wage and the prevailing wage?
>
> • \[ \] Is the employer prepared to file and post or otherwise provide notice of the LCA at the worksite?
>
> • \[ \] Has the employer confirmed that no labor dispute, strike, or lockout exists at the worksite in the relevant occupational classification?

**Cap and Timing:**

> • \[ \] Is the candidate currently in valid H-1B status with another employer (cap-exempt change of employer)?
>
> • \[ \] If the candidate is cap-subject, has the employer completed or initiated registration in the USCIS electronic registration system for the applicable fiscal year?
>
> • \[ \] Is the target start date aligned with the October 1 fiscal year start, or does the timeline require premium processing or other expedited handling?

**Fees and Budget:**

> • \[ \] Has the employer budgeted for total government filing fees of \$3,060 per H-1B petition (for employers with 26 or more full-time equivalent employees)?
>
> • \[ \] If premium processing is needed, has the additional \$2,805 premium processing fee been budgeted?
>
> • \[ \] Has the \$215 per-beneficiary registration fee been accounted for separately from petition-stage filing fees?

This checklist should be completed and returned to the assigned Brightfield & Novak LLP attorney for each prospective H-1B candidate prior to the initiation of the LCA and petition preparation process.

**[Section 10: Common Pitfalls and Practice Tips]{.underline}**

Based on the firm\'s experience with Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc.\'s prior H-1B filings and broader practice trends, the following common pitfalls and practice recommendations should be observed in preparing future H-1B petitions.

**Specialty Occupation RFEs.** USCIS frequently issues Requests for Evidence challenging whether a position qualifies as a specialty occupation, particularly for positions with broad or general-sounding titles such as \"systems analyst,\" \"IT consultant,\" \"programmer analyst,\" or \"business analyst.\" Five of Aethon\'s seven H-1B denials over the past five fiscal years involved specialty occupation challenges, underscoring the importance of precise position descriptions. For Aethon\'s future filings, specific engineering titles --- such as \"Senior ASIC Design Engineer,\" \"Firmware Engineer --- Embedded Systems,\" or \"Principal Research Scientist, Semiconductor Physics\" --- should be used, accompanied by detailed duty descriptions that reference specific technical competencies, design tools, programming languages, and the specialized knowledge required for the role. Position descriptions should explicitly connect each major duty to the relevant body of specialized knowledge and explain why the duty requires at least a bachelor\'s degree in the identified specialty.

**Third-Party Worksite Issues.** If any of Aethon\'s H-1B engineers will be placed at client or partner facilities --- for example, at foundry partners\' fabrication sites for design verification, process qualification, or yield analysis activities --- additional documentation will be required to demonstrate that Aethon maintains sufficient control over the worker\'s employment at the third-party location. The petition should include contracts or work orders between Aethon and the third-party site, a detailed itinerary specifying the duration and nature of the off-site work, and evidence of Aethon\'s supervisory structure (e.g., reporting relationships, performance evaluation authority). Failure to provide adequate third-party worksite documentation was a contributing factor in two of Aethon\'s prior denials.

**Wage Level Disputes.** The DOL wage level assigned to a position on the LCA has been a subject of increasing scrutiny. Designating a Level I wage for a position that involves complex, independent work or supervisory responsibilities can trigger both DOL audits and USCIS RFEs. The firm recommends that Aethon request Level II or Level III designations for its positions, consistent with the duties, experience requirements, and degree of independent judgment expected of the candidates being sponsored. The salary ranges Aethon has proposed should support Level II and Level III designations without difficulty.

**Timing and Registration Deadlines.** Given that Aethon\'s target start dates for the planned hires are Q3 2025 and later, cap registration during the March 2025 registration period is critical for all cap-subject candidates. Missing the registration deadline would result in a one-year delay --- the next available filing opportunity would be March 2026 for an October 2026 start date. The firm will coordinate with Priya Surendran to ensure all registrations are prepared and submitted within the registration window.

**Historical Approval Rate.** Aethon\'s 78% H-1B approval rate (37 approvals out of 47 filings) is below the national average for technology sector employers, which has historically ranged from approximately 85% to 95% depending on company size and position type. The firm recommends a pre-filing review protocol in which each position description and supporting documentation package is reviewed by immigration counsel before submission, with particular attention to the specialty occupation analysis and employer-employee relationship documentation. This pre-filing review process should improve approval rates and reduce the incidence of costly and time-consuming RFEs.

**Coordination with Other Visa Categories.** For candidates such as Dr. Wei-Lin Chang and Dr. Katarina Breitner, who have existing employment relationships with Aethon\'s foreign subsidiaries, counsel should evaluate whether an L-1B intracompany transferee petition or an O-1 extraordinary ability petition may be strategically preferable to H-1B. The L-1 and O-1 categories are not subject to the H-1B cap lottery, offer different initial validity periods, and may present stronger substantive cases for candidates with significant specialized knowledge or extraordinary accomplishments. H-1B should be considered as a parallel or backup strategy for these candidates, but the primary approach should be determined after a full assessment of each candidate\'s qualifications, timeline, and long-term immigration objectives.

28	
29	**General Purpose.** The L-1 classification allows U.S. employers to transfer qualified employees from affiliated foreign offices to the United States. It also permits foreign companies that are in the process of establishing new offices in the U.S. to send qualifying employees to facilitate that establishment. The classification is employer-sponsored; the U.S. petitioner must file Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, on behalf of the beneficiary.
30	
31	**No Annual Cap.** Unlike the H-1B classification, the L-1 visa is *not* subject to annual numerical caps. There is no lottery or registration requirement, and petitions may be filed at any time during the year. This makes L-1 a particularly attractive option when H-1B cap slots are unavailable.
32	
33	**Relevance to Firm Client Matters.** The L-1 classification is directly relevant to companies with multinational operations. The firm currently represents Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc., a Delaware corporation with U.S. headquarters at 9401 Research Boulevard, Building C, Austin, TX 78759. Aethon maintains wholly-owned foreign subsidiaries, including Aethon Semiconductor Technologies Taiwan Ltd. (established September 2019; approximately 145 employees, based in Taipei) and Aethon Semiconductor GmbH (established January 2018; approximately 42 employees, based in Munich, Germany). Aethon currently has four employees in L-1B status and is evaluating additional transfers from its Taipei and Munich operations.
34	
35	**[Section 2: Qualifying Organizational Relationships]{.underline}**
36	
37	A threshold requirement for any L-1 petition is the existence of a \"qualifying relationship\" between the U.S. petitioning entity and the foreign entity where the beneficiary is or was employed. The regulations at 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii) define four types of qualifying relationships:
38	
39	**1. Parent-Subsidiary.** One entity owns or controls the other, either directly or indirectly. A \"subsidiary\" is defined under 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii)(G) as a firm, corporation, or other legal entity of which a parent owns, directly or indirectly, more than half of the entity and controls the entity; or owns, directly or indirectly, half of the entity and controls the entity; or owns, directly or indirectly, less than half of the entity but in fact controls the entity. The key inquiry is whether the parent entity exercises actual control over the subsidiary.
40	
41	**2. Branch Office.** An operating division or office of the same organization operating in a different location. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii)(J). A branch does not have separate legal personality from the parent organization but operates as an extension of it in another jurisdiction.
42	
43	**3. Affiliate.** Two entities are affiliates when they are both owned and controlled by the same parent or individual, or by the same group of individuals, each owning and controlling the entities in approximately the same share or proportion. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii)(L). Affiliate relationships require careful documentation, particularly where multiple shareholders or partners are involved, as USCIS will examine whether the controlling individuals hold their ownership interests in substantially similar proportions across both entities.
44	
45	**4. Joint Venture.** A joint venture entity may qualify if the joint venture participants exercise sufficient control. This determination is highly fact-specific, and joint venture arrangements often require additional evidentiary support to demonstrate that the qualifying organizations maintain the requisite degree of ownership and control.
46	
47	**Practical Application.** Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc. (the U.S. parent) has a clear qualifying parent-subsidiary relationship with both Aethon Semiconductor Technologies Taiwan Ltd. and Aethon Semiconductor GmbH, as both are wholly-owned subsidiaries. Wholly-owned subsidiaries straightforwardly satisfy the qualifying relationship requirement, and documentation of this relationship is typically uncomplicated.
48	
49	**Evidence of Qualifying Relationship.** Petitioners should be prepared to submit organizational charts, articles of incorporation, stock certificates or membership interest records, annual reports, operating agreements, wire transfer records evidencing capitalization or intercompany transfers, and tax returns. For Aethon matters, financial verification documentation is prepared by Stonecrest Accounting Group LLP, the company\'s auditor of record.
50	
51	**Ongoing Requirement.** The qualifying relationship must exist both at the time the petition is filed and must be maintained throughout the L-1 beneficiary\'s authorized period of stay. If the qualifying relationship is severed --- for example, through a divestiture or corporate restructuring --- the L-1 status of affected beneficiaries may be jeopardized.
52	
53	**\"Doing Business\" Requirement.** Both the U.S. entity and the foreign entity must be \"doing business\" during the pendency of the L-1 status. \"Doing business\" is defined as the regular, systematic, and continuous provision of goods and/or services by a qualifying organization. The mere presence of an agent or representative office in the United States does not satisfy this requirement. Both entities must be actively engaged in commercial operations.
54	
55	**[Section 3: Beneficiary Eligibility --- General Requirements]{.underline}**
56	
57	**One-Year Foreign Employment Requirement.** The beneficiary must have been employed by the qualifying foreign entity in a managerial, executive, or specialized knowledge capacity for one continuous year within the three years immediately preceding the filing of the L-1 petition. If the beneficiary is already in the United States, the relevant three-year window is measured from the date of the beneficiary\'s last admission. See INA § 214(c)(2)(A); 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(i).
58	
59	The term \"continuous\" does not require uninterrupted physical presence abroad. Brief trips to the United States or other countries for business or pleasure do not break the continuity of the one-year employment period. However, the beneficiary must have been employed by the foreign affiliate for an unbroken year, and any absences from employment (as opposed to absences from the foreign country) could raise issues. The one-year period must have been spent outside the United States working for the qualifying organization. Time spent in the United States in lawful status for the qualifying organization generally does *not* count toward the one-year foreign employment requirement, though such U.S. time may toll the three-year lookback window under certain circumstances.
60

As of Q3 2025 (the earliest target start date for transfer), Dr. Chang will have accumulated over four years of continuous employment with the Taipei subsidiary, clearly satisfying the one-year requirement.

Alternative visa categories, such as H-1B, should be explored for Mr. Malhotra.
68	
69	**U.S. Position Requirement.** In addition to satisfying the one-year foreign employment requirement, the beneficiary must be coming to the United States to serve in a managerial, executive, or specialized knowledge capacity with the petitioning organization. The nature of the U.S. role is evaluated independently from the nature of the foreign employment, though the underlying qualifying relationship must connect both positions.
70	
71	**[Section 4: L-1A --- Managers and Executives]{.underline}**
72	
73	**4.1 Managerial Capacity Defined**
74	
75	The term \"managerial capacity\" is defined at INA § 101(a)(44)(A) and 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii)(B). To qualify as serving in a managerial capacity, an individual must meet the following criteria:
76	
77	> • Manages the organization, or a department, subdivision, function, or component of the organization;
78	>
79	> • Supervises and controls the work of other supervisory, professional, or managerial employees, *or* manages an essential function within the organization or a department or division of the organization;
80	>
81	> • Has the authority to hire and fire or recommend personnel actions (such as promotion and leave authorization) with respect to directly supervised employees, *or* if managing a function, operates at a senior level within the organizational hierarchy or with respect to the function managed; and
82	>
83	> • Exercises discretion over the day-to-day operations of the activity or function for which the employee has authority.
84	
85	**Function Manager Concept.** An individual who manages an \"essential function\" of the organization may qualify for L-1A classification even without direct supervisory authority over subordinate employees. However, USCIS closely scrutinizes function manager claims, and they are a frequent source of Requests for Evidence (\"RFEs\"). Petitioners asserting function manager eligibility should provide detailed evidence regarding the scope and complexity of the function, the seniority of the individual\'s position within the organizational hierarchy, and the degree of discretion exercised.
86	
87	**Practical Note.** Aethon\'s planned expansion includes three managerial-level positions with a salary range of \$190,000--\$240,000. These positions may qualify for L-1A classification provided that the candidates have qualifying foreign employment and will serve in a genuinely managerial or executive capacity in the United States.
88	
89	**4.2 Executive Capacity Defined**
90	
91	The term \"executive capacity\" is defined at INA § 101(a)(44)(B) and 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii)(C). An individual serves in an executive capacity if he or she:
92	
93	> • Directs the management of the organization or a major component or function of the organization;
94	>
95	> • Establishes the goals and policies of the organization, component, or function;
96	>
97	> • Exercises wide latitude in discretionary decision-making; and
98	>
99	> • Receives only general supervision or direction from higher-level executives, the board of directors, or stockholders of the organization.
100	
101	**Distinction from Managerial Capacity.** Executive capacity involves higher-level responsibilities such as goal-setting and policy-making for the organization or a major component thereof. Managerial capacity, by contrast, centers on operational oversight --- supervising employees or managing functions on a day-to-day basis. In practice, the two definitions frequently overlap, and a petition may allege both managerial and executive capacity in the alternative. USCIS will evaluate the evidence under both standards where both are asserted.
102	
103	**4.3 Duration of Status --- L-1A**
104	
105	**Existing Office Petitions.** For transfers to an established U.S. office (one that has been doing business for at least one year), L-1A petitions may be approved for an initial period of stay of up to three years. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(7)(i)(A)(1). Extensions are granted in increments of up to two years.
106	
107	**Maximum Stay.** The maximum aggregate period of stay in L-1A status is seven years. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(12)(i). Time previously spent in H, L, or certain other nonimmigrant statuses may count against the seven-year maximum. Beneficiaries may be eligible to \"recapture\" time spent physically outside the United States during their L-1 stay, effectively extending their eligibility.
108	
109	**New Office Petitions.** For new office L-1A petitions, the initial approval period is limited to one year. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(7)(i)(A)(2). Additional requirements applicable to new office petitions are discussed in Section 7 below.
110	
111	**[Section 5: L-1B --- Specialized Knowledge Workers]{.underline}**
112	
113	**5.1 Specialized Knowledge Defined**
114	
115	**Statutory and Regulatory Basis.** The specialized knowledge standard is set forth in INA § 214(c)(2)(B) and further defined at 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii)(D).
116	
117	**Definition.** \"Specialized knowledge\" means knowledge possessed by an individual of the petitioning organization\'s product, service, research, equipment, techniques, management, or other interests and its application in international markets, or an advanced level of knowledge or expertise in the organization\'s processes and procedures. The statute and USCIS guidance recognize two forms of specialized knowledge:
118	
119	1\. **Special knowledge** --- knowledge of the petitioning organization\'s products, services, research, equipment, techniques, management, or other interests, and its application in international markets; and
120	
121	2\. **Advanced knowledge** --- an advanced level of knowledge or expertise in the organization\'s processes and procedures.
122	
123	To qualify for L-1B classification, the beneficiary must demonstrate that he or she possesses **both** special knowledge of the petitioning organization\'s products, services, and interests **and** advanced knowledge of the organization\'s processes and procedures. The beneficiary\'s knowledge must be distinguishable from that commonly held by others in the industry, and must reflect a depth of understanding that was gained through significant and meaningful experience with the petitioning organization.
124	
125	**Evaluative Factors.** USCIS examines whether the beneficiary\'s knowledge is not commonly held in the relevant industry, whether the knowledge was gained through significant prior experience with the employer, and whether the knowledge is valuable to the employer\'s competitive position in the marketplace. The 2015 L-1B Policy Memorandum (PM-602-0111) provides additional adjudicative guidance and identifies the following non-exhaustive factors:
126	
127	> • Whether the beneficiary possesses knowledge of foreign operating conditions that is of significant value to the petitioner\'s U.S. operations;
128	>
129	> • Whether the beneficiary has been employed abroad in a capacity involving significant assignments that have enhanced the employer\'s productivity, competitiveness, image, or financial position;
130	>
131	> • Whether the beneficiary\'s claimed specialized knowledge normally can be gained only through prior experience with the petitioning organization; and
132	>
133	> • Whether the beneficiary possesses knowledge of a product or process that cannot be easily transferred or taught to another individual.
134	
135	No single factor is dispositive, and USCIS adjudicators are directed to evaluate the totality of the evidence presented.
136	
137	**Practical Application.** Aethon currently has four employees in L-1B status, demonstrating established use of this classification. Dr. Wei-Lin Chang (Senior Design Engineer at the Taipei subsidiary since June 2021, with deep knowledge of Aethon\'s proprietary chip design verification and testing processes, six published papers, and two patents) is a strong L-1B candidate. Dr. Katarina Breitner (Principal Researcher at the Munich subsidiary since March 2020, with expertise in Aethon\'s advanced node process development and photonics research, fourteen published papers, and three patents) is also a potential L-1B candidate, though Dr. Breitner\'s profile and seniority may additionally support an L-1A classification as a function manager.
138	
139	**5.2 Duration of Status --- L-1B**
140	
141	**Existing Office Petitions.** L-1B petitions for transfers to an established U.S. office may be approved for an initial period of stay of up to three years, consistent with the L-1A timeline. Extensions are granted in increments of up to two years.
142	
143	**Maximum Stay.** The maximum aggregate period of stay in L-1B status is five years. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(12)(ii). This is two years shorter than the seven-year maximum for L-1A beneficiaries. Time previously spent in H, L, or certain other nonimmigrant statuses may count against the five-year limit.
144	
145	**New Office Petitions.** For new office L-1B petitions, the initial approval period is limited to one year, consistent with the new office rules applicable to L-1A.
146	
147	**One-Year Bar.** After the five-year maximum is reached, the beneficiary must reside and be physically present outside the United States for a continuous period of one year before becoming eligible for a new L-1 or H-1B petition. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(12)(iii). Planning for this limitation should be incorporated into any long-term transfer strategy.
148	
149	**[Section 6: Petitioner/Employer Requirements]{.underline}**
150	
151	The U.S. petitioner initiates the L-1 process by filing Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, with the appropriate USCIS service center or electronically via the myUSCIS online portal. The petitioner must establish the following:
152	
153	1\. A qualifying relationship between the U.S. entity and the foreign entity (see Section 2);
154	
155	2\. That both entities are or will be doing business as employers engaged in the regular, systematic, and continuous provision of goods and/or services;
156	
157	3\. That the beneficiary meets the one-year qualifying foreign employment requirement (see Section 3); and
158	
159	4\. That the beneficiary will be employed in a qualifying capacity --- managerial, executive, or specialized knowledge --- in the United States.
160	
161	**Supporting Documentation.** The petition should be accompanied by a robust evidentiary record. While the specific documents required will vary by case, commonly submitted evidence includes: corporate documents and stock records demonstrating the qualifying relationship; annual reports and audited financial statements (Aethon\'s auditor of record is Stonecrest Accounting Group LLP); tax returns, contracts, and commercial leases demonstrating that both entities are doing business; employment verification letters, pay stubs, and organizational charts evidencing the beneficiary\'s foreign employment; and detailed job descriptions, organizational charts, and, where appropriate, expert opinion letters describing the nature and requirements of the proposed U.S. position.

183	**[Section 7: New Office L-1 Petitions]{.underline}**
184	
185	**7.1 Overview.** A \"new office\" petition is one filed by or on behalf of a U.S. entity that has been doing business for less than one year. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(1)(ii)(F). New office petitions are subject to additional evidentiary requirements and a shorter initial approval period than standard L-1 petitions. This provision is frequently used when a foreign company is establishing its first U.S. presence or when an existing U.S. company is opening a new subsidiary or branch office that will employ the L-1 beneficiary.
186	
187	While Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc. has been in business since 2016 and its U.S. operations are well established (612 U.S. employees; approximately \$248 million in annual revenue for FY2024), this section is included for completeness. The new office provisions could become relevant if Aethon establishes additional U.S. entities or subsidiaries in the future.
188	
189	**7.2 Evidentiary Requirements for New Office Petitions**
190	
191	In addition to the standard L-1 evidentiary requirements described in Section 6, a new office petitioner must submit the following:
192	
193	> • Evidence that the petitioner has secured sufficient physical premises to commence doing business (e.g., a signed lease agreement or property purchase agreement);
194	>
195	> • Evidence of the scope of the proposed business entity, including a detailed business plan and financial projections;
196	>
197	> • Evidence of the organizational structure of the foreign entity.
198	
199	For **L-1A new office petitions** specifically, the regulations require additional documentation:
200	
201	> • A detailed business plan demonstrating projected staffing levels and organizational structure for the proposed U.S. office;
202	>
203	> • Evidence that the proposed U.S. entity will grow to a size sufficient to support the beneficiary\'s managerial or executive role within a reasonable timeframe;
204	>
205	> • Financial evidence demonstrating adequate capitalization, including projected revenues and proof of investment or funding commitments.
206	
207	For **L-1B new office petitions**, the petitioner must establish that the new office will require the specialized knowledge services of the beneficiary. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(3)(v) and (vi).
208	
209	**7.3 Initial Approval Period and Extensions**
210	
211	**Initial Approval.** New office L-1 petitions --- both L-1A and L-1B --- are initially approved for a maximum period of one year. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(7)(i)(A)(2). This contrasts with the three-year initial approval period available for petitions involving established U.S. offices.
212	
213	**Extension Requirements.** When filing an extension after the initial one-year period, the petitioner must demonstrate that the U.S. entity has been doing business for the preceding year and must provide updated evidentiary support. New office L-1A petitions are initially approved for one year. At the time of extension, the petitioner must demonstrate that the U.S. entity has been doing business and provide updated organizational and financial documentation. This includes current organizational charts showing the beneficiary\'s position within the corporate hierarchy, payroll records for U.S. employees, and recent tax filings or financial statements demonstrating ongoing commercial operations.
214	
215	**Practical Note.** While Aethon\'s U.S. headquarters is well established, the firm has never filed an L-1A petition on Aethon\'s behalf. Counsel should carefully review all applicable requirements --- including the new office provisions --- if Aethon establishes any additional U.S. subsidiaries, branch offices, or affiliates in the future and seeks to transfer managerial or executive personnel to those entities.

217	**[Section 8: L-1 Blanket Petitions]{.underline}**
218	
219	**8.1 Overview and Purpose**
220	
221	An L-1 blanket petition allows qualifying multinational organizations to obtain pre-approval from USCIS, enabling individual L-1 beneficiaries to apply for visa issuance directly at a U.S. consular post abroad without the need for a separate Form I-129 individual petition for each transferee. This mechanism significantly streamlines the transfer process for organizations that engage in frequent intracompany transfers. Blanket petitions cover both L-1A and L-1B classifications. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(4).
222	
223	**8.2 Eligibility Criteria for Blanket Petitions**
224	
225	To qualify for an L-1 blanket petition, the petitioner and its qualifying organizations must establish **all three** of the following criteria:
226	
227	**(a)** The petitioner and each qualifying organization are engaged in commercial trade or services and have an office in the United States that has been doing business for one year or more;
228	
229	**(b)** The petitioner has three or more domestic and foreign branches, subsidiaries, or affiliates; and
230	
231	**(c)** The petitioner and the qualifying organizations have combined annual sales of at least **\$25 million**, **or** have a United States workforce of at least **1,000 employees**.
232	
233	See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(4)(i).
234	
235	**Aethon Blanket Petition Analysis.** Applying these criteria to Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc.:
236	
237	> • **Criterion (a):** Aethon has maintained a U.S. office since its founding in 2016, well in excess of the one-year minimum. *Met.*
238	>
239	> • **Criterion (b):** Aethon has at least three qualifying entities: (1) Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc. (U.S. parent), (2) Aethon Semiconductor Technologies Taiwan Ltd. (Taipei; established September 2019), and (3) Aethon Semiconductor GmbH (Munich; established January 2018). *Met.*
240	>
241	> • **Criterion (c):** Aethon\'s annual revenue is approximately \$248 million (FY2024), which substantially exceeds the \$25 million sales threshold. (Note that Aethon\'s U.S. workforce of 612 employees falls below the 1,000-employee alternative; the sales threshold is the applicable path.) *Met.*
242	
243	**Conclusion.** Aethon appears to satisfy all eligibility criteria for an L-1 blanket petition. Pursuing blanket petition approval could significantly streamline future transfers from the Taipei and Munich offices, eliminating the need for individual I-129 filings for each transferee and allowing candidates to apply directly at U.S. consulates abroad.
244	
245	**8.3 Blanket Petition Filing and Validity**
246	
247	Blanket petitions are filed using Form I-129S along with supporting corporate documentation. An initial blanket petition, once approved, is valid for three years. Upon timely extension, blanket petitions receive indefinite validity so long as the qualifying criteria continue to be met.
248	
249	Individual L-1 beneficiaries covered by an approved blanket petition apply at a U.S. consulate using Form I-129S and supporting documentation. Notably, beneficiaries seeking L-1B classification under a blanket petition must hold a bachelor\'s degree or its foreign equivalent --- a requirement that does not apply to individually filed L-1B petitions. See 8 CFR 214.2(l)(4)(ii). This is an important distinction that should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
250	
251	**Filing Fees.** The blanket petition itself requires a base filing fee of \$460 plus the \$500 fraud prevention and detection fee, totaling \$960. Individual beneficiaries applying at the consulate under the blanket petition are subject to a \$500 anti-fraud fee per beneficiary.

281	**[Section 10: Practical Considerations and Common Pitfalls]{.underline}**
282	
283	**RFE Trends.** USCIS has increased scrutiny of L-1B petitions in recent years. The most common Request for Evidence issues include:
284	
285	> • Failure to adequately distinguish the beneficiary\'s specialized knowledge from knowledge commonly held in the industry;
286	>
287	> • Insufficient documentation of the qualifying organizational relationship;
288	>
289	> • Vague, boilerplate, or overly generic job descriptions that fail to convey the specialized nature of the position;
290	>
291	> • Failure to explain why the specialized knowledge cannot be readily transferred to a U.S. worker through reasonable training.
292	
293	Practitioners should anticipate these issues during petition preparation and proactively address them in the initial filing.
294	
295	**L-1A Function Manager Pitfalls.** Claims of managing an \"essential function\" without direct supervisory authority over subordinate employees are closely scrutinized by USCIS. Petitioners should provide detailed evidence of the scope, complexity, and organizational significance of the function managed, the beneficiary\'s level of seniority, and the degree of discretionary authority exercised.
296	
297	**Dual Intent.** The L-1 is a dual-intent visa category. Beneficiaries may pursue lawful permanent residence (a green card) while maintaining L-1 nonimmigrant status. This is a significant advantage over certain other nonimmigrant classifications (e.g., TN status) where immigrant intent can be problematic.
298	
299	**Immigrant Visa Pathways.** L-1A holders may be eligible for EB-1C (multinational manager/executive) immigrant classification, which does not require PERM labor certification --- a substantial advantage in terms of processing time and cost. L-1B holders do not have a direct immigrant pathway equivalent and typically pursue EB-2 (advanced degree professional) or EB-3 (skilled worker) immigrant classification, both of which generally require PERM labor certification.
300	
301	**Change of Status and Extensions.** L-1 beneficiaries may extend their status or change to another nonimmigrant classification from within the United States by filing a new or amended Form I-129 with USCIS.
302	
303	**Annual Reporting.** USCIS may request annualized data on L-1 usage. Employers should maintain accurate and contemporaneous records of all L-1 employees, including dates of entry, expiration dates, and position information.
304	
305	**Wage Considerations.** While L-1 does not impose the same prevailing wage requirements as H-1B (no Labor Condition Application is required), the employer must pay the L-1 beneficiary a wage consistent with the offered position. Employers should document that the offered salary is reasonable for the position, level, and geographic location to avoid any inference that the L-1 program is being used to undercut domestic wage standards.
306

The planned expansion includes three managerial-level positions (salary range \$190,000--\$240,000) that may warrant L-1A classification, along with potential additional L-1B filings for specialized engineers transferring from Taipei and Munich. Principal Researcher at the Munich subsidiary since March 2020, overseeing advanced node process development and photonics research; fourteen published papers and three patents. Dr. Breitner\'s profile may support classification as a \"function manager\" for L-1A purposes.
