1	**[EMPLOYMENT-BASED IMMIGRANT & NONIMMIGRANT EXTRAORDINARY ABILITY CATEGORIES]{.underline}**
2	
3	**Internal Guidance Document** **Brightfield & Novak LLP Immigration Practice Group**
4	
5	Document Identifier:
6	
7	Prepared by: Marcus Novak, Immigration Practice Group Lead Brightfield & Novak LLP 3200 Guadalupe Street, Suite 1100 Austin, TX 78705
8	
9	Last Updated: January 2025
10	
11	ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT --- FOR INTERNAL USE ONLY. This document is intended for use by Brightfield & Novak LLP attorneys and authorized client personnel. Not for distribution. Unauthorized reproduction, dissemination, or disclosure of this document or any information contained herein is strictly prohibited and may violate applicable rules of professional conduct. This document incorporates USCIS Policy Manual guidance through December 2024.
12	
13	Right-click to update Table of Contents
14	
15	**[Section 1: Introduction and Purpose]{.underline}**
16	
17	This document provides a comprehensive overview of the employment-based nonimmigrant and immigrant visa categories available to individuals of extraordinary ability, outstanding achievement, or advanced qualifications in the sciences, arts, business, education, and athletics. The guidance herein is designed to serve as a practical reference tool for attorneys and staff evaluating potential visa strategies on behalf of our firm\'s corporate clients and individual beneficiaries.
18	
19	The categories covered in this document are as follows: the O-1A nonimmigrant visa (extraordinary ability in the sciences, business, education, or athletics), the O-1B nonimmigrant visa (extraordinary ability or achievement in the arts), the EB-1A first preference immigrant visa (extraordinary ability), the EB-1B first preference immigrant visa (outstanding professors and researchers), the EB-2 second preference immigrant visa (members of professions holding advanced degrees or persons of exceptional ability), and the EB-2 National Interest Waiver (NIW). Each category is discussed with reference to its statutory and regulatory basis, eligibility criteria, evidentiary requirements, filing procedures, and practical considerations relevant to our current client engagements.
20	
21	This document is intended for use by Brightfield & Novak LLP immigration attorneys, paralegals, and authorized client human resources representatives. It should be read in conjunction with DOC*001 (H-1B Regulatory Summary), DOC*002 (L-1 Intracompany Transferee Summary), DOC*003 (USCIS Policy Guidance Memorandum), and DOC*005 (Visa Category Selection Flowchart, developed by Marcus Novak in 2022). Readers are encouraged to consult those companion documents for complete coverage of the firm\'s immigration practice guidance materials.
22	
23	Throughout this document, we reference our client Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc. (a Delaware corporation headquartered at 9401 Research Boulevard, Building C, Austin, TX 78759) as a representative petitioner for illustrative examples. Aethon currently has two employees in O-1B nonimmigrant status. As communicated by Aethon\'s Vice President of Human Resources in September 2024, Aethon plans to hire approximately thirty-five foreign nationals from Q3 2025 through Q4 2026, including five research scientists and three managerial-level positions, some of whom may qualify for the visa categories covered in this document.
24	
25	Representative candidates for the categories discussed herein include: Dr. Katarina Breitner (German national, Principal Researcher at Aethon Semiconductor GmbH in Munich; holder of fourteen published papers, three patents, and journal peer review experience) and Dr. Wei-Lin Chang (Taiwanese national, Senior Design Engineer at Aethon Semiconductor Technologies Taiwan Ltd. in Taipei; holder of six published papers and two patents). These candidates are referenced throughout the document to illustrate how the various eligibility criteria may apply in practice.
26	
27	**[Section 2: O-1 Nonimmigrant Visa --- Individuals of Extraordinary Ability or Achievement]{.underline}**
28	
29	**[2.1 Overview]{.underline}**
30	
31	The O-1 nonimmigrant visa classification is established under Section 101(a)(15)(O) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and is further governed by the regulations set forth at 8 CFR 214.2(o). The O-1 classification is available to individuals who possess extraordinary ability in their respective fields or who have achieved extraordinary accomplishment in the arts, and who are coming to the United States temporarily to continue working in their area of extraordinary ability or achievement.
32	
33	The O-1 category is divided into two sub-categories. O-1A covers individuals of extraordinary ability in the sciences, business, education, or athletics. O-1B covers individuals of extraordinary ability or achievement in the arts, including the motion picture and television industry. The distinction between these two sub-categories is significant, as the evidentiary standards and specific criteria differ between them.
34	
35	The O-1 is an employer-sponsored nonimmigrant visa. A U.S. employer or authorized agent must file Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, on behalf of the beneficiary. There is no annual cap on the number of O-1 visas that may be issued in a given fiscal year, which distinguishes the O-1 from the numerically limited H-1B category. The initial period of stay for an O-1 beneficiary is up to three years, with extensions available in one-year increments for the duration of the event or activity for which the beneficiary was admitted. Filing fees consist of the Form I-129 base fee, and premium processing is available through Form I-907 for an additional fee. An advisory opinion from a peer group, labor organization, or management organization in the beneficiary\'s field of endeavor is required as part of the petition.
36	
37	As noted above, Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc. currently has two employees in O-1B nonimmigrant status.
38	
39	**[2.2 O-1A --- Extraordinary Ability in the Sciences, Business, Education, or Athletics]{.underline}**
40	
41	To qualify for O-1A classification in the sciences, the beneficiary must demonstrate extraordinary ability by sustained national or international acclaim and must be coming to the United States to continue work in the area of extraordinary ability. The petition must be accompanied by evidence that the beneficiary has received sustained national or international acclaim and has been recognized for achievements in the field of endeavor.
42	
43	Extraordinary ability in the field of science is demonstrated by a level of distinction indicating that the beneficiary is one of a small percentage who have risen to the very top of the field. This is a high standard and requires substantial documentary evidence to support the claim. USCIS will evaluate the totality of the evidence submitted in determining whether the beneficiary meets this threshold.
44	
45	The beneficiary must meet at least three of the following evidentiary criteria, or provide evidence of a one-time major internationally recognized achievement (such as a Nobel Prize, Pulitzer Prize, or Oscar):
46	
47	> 1\. Nominations for, or receipt of, significant national or international awards or prizes in the particular field, such as an Academy Award, Emmy, Grammy, or Director\'s Guild Award;
48	>
49	> 2\. Documentation of the beneficiary\'s membership in associations in the field for which classification is sought, which require outstanding achievements of their members, as judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or fields;
50	>
51	> 3\. Published material in professional or major trade publications or major media about the beneficiary, relating to the beneficiary\'s work in the field for which classification is sought;
52	>
53	> 4\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s participation, either individually or on a panel, as a judge of the work of others in the same or an allied field of specification for which classification is sought;
54	>
55	> 5\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s original scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major significance in the field;
56	>
57	> 6\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s authorship of scholarly articles in professional journals or other major media in the field for which classification is sought;
58	>
59	> 7\. A record of major commercial or critically acclaimed successes in the performing arts, as shown by box office receipts or record, cassette, compact disk, or video sales, or other indicators of commercial success;
60	>
61	> 8\. Evidence that the beneficiary has either commanded or currently commands a high salary or other significantly high remuneration for services in relation to others in the field, as evidenced by contracts or other reliable evidence.
62	
63	The beneficiary must satisfy at least three of these eight criteria, or alternatively may demonstrate eligibility through evidence of a one-time major internationally recognized achievement. Examples of such one-time achievements include the Nobel Prize, the Pulitzer Prize, or an Oscar. Where the beneficiary has received such an award, additional evidence may not be required, though USCIS retains discretion to request further documentation.
64	
65	For Aethon\'s research scientists and engineers, the O-1A category may be appropriate for individuals with extraordinary track records. Dr. Katarina Breitner, for example, has fourteen published papers, three patents, and has served as a journal peer reviewer, which may support several of the above criteria. In particular, her journal peer review activity supports criterion number four (judging the work of others), her patents and published research support criterion number five (original contributions of major significance), and her fourteen publications support criterion number six (authorship of scholarly articles). Additional evidence of awards, media coverage, salary data, or membership in selective professional associations would further strengthen the petition.
66	
67	**[2.3 O-1B --- Extraordinary Ability or Achievement in the Arts]{.underline}**
68	
69	The O-1B nonimmigrant classification covers individuals who possess extraordinary ability or achievement in the arts, including those working in the motion picture and television industry. The standard for O-1B differs from the standard applied to O-1A petitions. For O-1B in the arts generally, the beneficiary must demonstrate \"distinction,\" which is defined as a high level of achievement in the field of the arts evidenced by a degree of skill and recognition substantially above that ordinarily encountered to the extent that a person described as prominent is renowned, leading, or well-known in the field of arts. For the motion picture and television industry specifically, the beneficiary must demonstrate \"a very high level of accomplishment evidenced by a degree of skill and recognition significantly above that ordinarily encountered to the extent that the person is recognized as outstanding, notable, or leading in the motion picture and/or television field.\"
70	
71	The O-1B evidentiary criteria differ from the O-1A criteria discussed above. The O-1B criteria are set forth in 8 CFR 214.2(o)(3)(iv) and include considerations specific to the arts, such as evidence of the beneficiary\'s leading or starring role in productions or events with a distinguished reputation, critical reviews or other published material demonstrating the beneficiary\'s acclaim in the field, and evidence of a record of major commercial or critically acclaimed successes. Because the O-1B criteria are tailored to evaluating artistic achievement, practitioners should take care to apply the appropriate regulatory criteria when preparing either an O-1A or O-1B petition.
72	
73	O-1B is generally not applicable to Aethon\'s current hiring plans, which focus on science and engineering professionals working in semiconductor technology and related fields. The two existing O-1B employees at Aethon are not the subject of this guidance document. For Aethon\'s planned hires in research science and engineering, the O-1A classification and its corresponding evidentiary criteria should be the focus of any nonimmigrant extraordinary ability petition strategy.
74	
75	**[2.4 O-1 Practical Considerations]{.underline}**
76	
77	Several practical considerations apply when preparing and filing O-1 petitions for Aethon\'s prospective employees and other firm clients.
78	
79	**Advisory Opinion Requirement.** Every O-1 petition must be accompanied by a written advisory opinion from an appropriate peer group, labor organization, or management organization in the beneficiary\'s field of endeavor. The advisory opinion must evaluate the beneficiary\'s qualifications and the nature of the proposed employment. If no appropriate peer group, labor organization, or management organization exists for the specific field, USCIS may accept a letter from an expert in the field in lieu of a formal advisory opinion. Practitioners should identify the appropriate advisory body early in the petition preparation process.
80	
81	**No Prevailing Wage Requirement.** Unlike the H-1B nonimmigrant classification, there is no prevailing wage requirement for O-1 petitions. The petitioning employer is not required to pay the beneficiary a wage at or above the prevailing wage for the occupation and area of employment. However, the salary offered may be relevant to the evidentiary criteria, particularly the criterion relating to high salary or remuneration.
82	
83	**Dual Intent.** O-1 visa holders may pursue permanent residence (i.e., apply for an immigrant visa or adjustment of status) without jeopardizing their nonimmigrant status. This dual intent doctrine makes the O-1 a strategic complement to immigrant visa petitions in the EB-1A or EB-1B categories. Beneficiaries who maintain valid O-1 status may lawfully remain in the United States while their I-140 immigrant petition and I-485 adjustment of status application are pending.
84	
85	**Filing Timeline.** We recommend filing O-1 petitions at least forty-five days before the intended start date of employment. If an expedited adjudication is necessary, premium processing through Form I-907 reduces the adjudication timeline to fifteen business days. Given the current processing climate and Aethon\'s planned hiring timeline extending through Q4 2026, early identification and preparation of O-1 candidates is advisable.
86	
87	**Bridge to Immigrant Visa.** The O-1 classification can serve as an effective bridge to the EB-1A or EB-1B immigrant visa categories. An approved O-1 petition, while not dispositive, constitutes relevant and persuasive evidence that the beneficiary has demonstrated extraordinary ability, which may support a subsequent I-140 petition. Aethon currently has two O-1B employees and may consider O-1A for some of the five planned research scientist hires during the Q3 2025 through Q4 2026 hiring period.
88	
89	**[Section 3: EB-1A --- Extraordinary Ability (First Preference Immigrant)]{.underline}**
90	
91	**[3.1 Overview and Statutory Basis]{.underline}**
92	
93	The EB-1A classification is the first preference employment-based immigrant visa category for individuals of extraordinary ability, established under INA § 203(b)(1)(A) and governed by the regulations at 8 CFR 204.5(h). The EB-1A category is reserved for individuals who have demonstrated extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics through sustained national or international acclaim, and whose achievements have been recognized in the field through extensive documentation.
94	
95	A significant advantage of the EB-1A classification is that no employer sponsorship is required. The beneficiary may file a self-petition using Form I-140, Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers. Additionally, the EB-1A category does not require labor certification through the PERM process, which eliminates the often lengthy and administratively burdensome labor market testing requirements that apply to other employment-based immigrant categories.
96	
97	The standard for EB-1A eligibility is \"extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics which has been demonstrated by sustained national or international acclaim.\" The beneficiary must be coming to the United States to continue work in the area of extraordinary ability, and the beneficiary\'s entry into the United States must prospectively benefit the United States. USCIS applies a two-step analysis in adjudicating EB-1A petitions: first, the adjudicator determines whether the beneficiary meets the requisite evidentiary criteria; second, the adjudicator conducts a final merits determination evaluating the totality of the evidence to determine whether the beneficiary has in fact achieved the level of sustained national or international acclaim required for this classification.
98	
99	**[3.2 EB-1A Evidentiary Criteria (Ten-Criteria List)]{.underline}**
100	
101	To establish eligibility for the EB-1A classification, the beneficiary must provide evidence of a one-time achievement --- specifically, a major, internationally recognized award, such as a Nobel Prize, Fields Medal, or comparable honor --- OR the beneficiary must provide evidence satisfying at least three of the following ten criteria enumerated at 8 CFR 204.5(h)(3):
102	
103	> 1\. Evidence of receipt of lesser nationally or internationally recognized prizes or awards for excellence in the field of endeavor;
104	>
105	> 2\. Evidence of membership in associations in the field which require outstanding achievements of their members, as judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or fields;
106	>
107	> 3\. Evidence of published material about the beneficiary in professional or major trade publications or other major media, relating to the beneficiary\'s work in the field of endeavor;
108	>
109	> 4\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s participation, either individually or on a panel, as a judge of the work of others in the same or an allied field of specialization;
110	>
111	> 5\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s original scientific, scholarly, artistic, athletic, or business-related contributions of major significance in the field;
112	>
113	> 6\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s authorship of scholarly articles in the field, in professional or major trade publications or other major media;
114	>
115	> 7\. Evidence of the display of the beneficiary\'s work in the field at artistic exhibitions or showcases;
116	>
117	> 8\. Evidence that the beneficiary has performed in a leading or critical role for organizations or establishments that have a distinguished reputation;
118	>
119	> 9\. Evidence that the beneficiary has commanded a high salary or other significantly high remuneration for services, in relation to others in the field;
120	>
121	> 10\. Evidence of commercial successes in the performing arts, as shown by box office receipts or record, cassette, compact disk, or video sales.
122	
123	The beneficiary need not satisfy all ten criteria. Rather, the beneficiary must present evidence meeting at least three of the ten criteria listed above, after which USCIS will proceed to the final merits determination discussed in Section 3.3 below. If the beneficiary has received a one-time major internationally recognized award, the three-criteria requirement may be waived entirely.
124	
125	**Practical Application for Aethon.** For semiconductor engineers and researchers, the most commonly applicable criteria are: original contributions of major significance (criterion 5), authorship of scholarly articles (criterion 6), judging the work of others such as through peer review of journal articles or grant applications (criterion 4), and performance in a leading or critical role for a distinguished organization (criterion 8). Awards in the semiconductor field (criterion 1), such as the IEEE Electron Device Society Awards or industry recognition from organizations like SEMI, and evidence of high salary or remuneration relative to others in the field (criterion 9) may also be viable depending on the beneficiary\'s profile. Criterion 7 (artistic exhibitions) and criterion 10 (commercial successes in the performing arts) are generally not applicable to STEM professionals.
126	
127	With respect to Dr. Katarina Breitner, her fourteen published papers, three patents, and journal peer review experience may satisfy criteria 4 (judging), 5 (original contributions), and 6 (authorship). Additional evidence of awards or recognition in the semiconductor or applied physics field, media coverage of her research, or membership in selective professional associations would further strengthen the petition and provide a broader evidentiary basis for the final merits determination. An analysis of Dr. Breitner\'s salary relative to comparable professionals in the semiconductor industry would also be useful for criterion 9.
128	
129	With respect to Dr. Wei-Lin Chang, his six published papers and two patents may satisfy criteria 5 (original contributions) and 6 (authorship), but additional evidence would be needed to meet the three-criterion threshold. We should explore whether Dr. Chang has served as a peer reviewer (criterion 4), received any industry awards or competitive grants (criterion 1), or can demonstrate a leading or critical role within Aethon\'s Taiwan operations (criterion 8). Citation analysis of Dr. Chang\'s published work would also be helpful in establishing the significance of his original contributions.
130	
131	It should be noted that in certain cases, the ten enumerated criteria may not readily apply to a beneficiary\'s occupation or field. Practitioners should carefully evaluate whether the listed criteria are adequate to capture the full scope of a beneficiary\'s achievements, particularly for professionals in emerging or highly specialized fields such as semiconductor process engineering, advanced node design, or photonics research, where accomplishments may take the form of proprietary innovations, industry standard contributions, or trade-secret-protected process developments that do not easily fit within the ten listed categories.
132	
133	**[3.3 Final Merits Determination]{.underline}**
134	
135	After establishing that the beneficiary satisfies at least three of the ten regulatory criteria (or has received a qualifying one-time major internationally recognized award), USCIS conducts a \"final merits determination\" in which the adjudicator evaluates the totality of the evidence submitted to determine whether the beneficiary has in fact demonstrated sustained national or international acclaim and is among the small percentage of individuals who have risen to the very top of their field of endeavor.
136	
137	The two-step analytical framework was established by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in *Kazarian v. USCIS*, 596 F.3d 1115 (9th Cir. 2010). Under the *Kazarian* framework, meeting three criteria alone does not guarantee approval. The adjudicator must assess, in the aggregate, whether the quality and nature of the evidence demonstrate that the beneficiary occupies the rarified position contemplated by the statute. Factors such as the prestige of the awards received, the selectivity of the associations to which the beneficiary belongs, the significance and impact of the beneficiary\'s original contributions, the prominence of the publications in which the beneficiary\'s work has appeared, and the reputation of the organizations for which the beneficiary has performed a leading or critical role are all relevant to this holistic assessment.
138	
139	As a practical matter, the strength and quality of the evidence matters significantly more than the sheer quantity. A beneficiary who satisfies five criteria with marginal evidence may fare worse than a beneficiary who satisfies three criteria with compelling, well-documented evidence. Practitioners should focus on developing the strongest possible evidentiary record for each criterion claimed and should prepare a persuasive narrative tying the evidence together in a manner that demonstrates sustained national or international acclaim.
140	
141	**[3.4 EB-1A Filing Information]{.underline}**
142	
143	The EB-1A petition is filed using Form I-140, Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers. The current base filing fee for Form I-140 is \$700, as of January 2025. Premium processing is available through Form I-907 for an additional fee of \$2,805, which provides an expedited adjudication timeline.
144	
145	No labor certification through the PERM process is required for the EB-1A classification. Self-petition is permitted, meaning the beneficiary may file the I-140 without an employer sponsor, though an employer may also file the petition on the beneficiary\'s behalf if it chooses to do so. The beneficiary\'s priority date is established upon the filing of the I-140 petition. Regular processing times for I-140 petitions currently range from approximately six to twelve months, depending on the USCIS service center. Premium processing guarantees a response within forty-five calendar days.
146	
147	**[Section 4: EB-1B --- Outstanding Professors and Researchers (First Preference Immigrant)]{.underline}**
148	
149	**[4.1 Overview and Statutory Basis]{.underline}**
150	
151	The EB-1B classification is the first preference employment-based immigrant visa category for outstanding professors and researchers, established under INA § 203(b)(1)(B) and governed by the regulations at 8 CFR 204.5(i). This category is designed for individuals who are recognized internationally as outstanding in a specific academic field and who are being recruited to the United States for a qualifying teaching or research position.
152	
153	Unlike the EB-1A classification, the EB-1B category requires employer sponsorship. The beneficiary cannot self-petition; rather, the prospective U.S. employer must file Form I-140 on behalf of the beneficiary. However, like EB-1A, the EB-1B classification does not require labor certification through the PERM process, which significantly streamlines the filing process and reduces the overall timeline to permanent residence.
154	
155	The standard for EB-1B eligibility is that the beneficiary must be \"recognized internationally as outstanding in a specific academic field.\" This standard, while rigorous, is generally considered somewhat lower than the EB-1A standard of \"extraordinary ability\" demonstrated by \"sustained national or international acclaim.\" The beneficiary must have accumulated at least three years of experience in teaching or research in the relevant academic field. This experience may have been gained at any institution or employer worldwide and need not be limited to U.S.-based experience.
156	
157	Additionally, the beneficiary must be entering the United States to take up a qualifying position: either a tenured or tenure-track teaching position at a university or institution of higher education, a comparable research position at a university or institution of higher education, or a comparable research position at a private employer. The nature of the position offered is a critical element of the EB-1B petition and must be documented with specificity.
158	
159	**[4.2 EB-1B Beneficiary Eligibility Criteria]{.underline}**
160	
161	To demonstrate international recognition as outstanding in a specific academic field, the beneficiary must provide evidence satisfying at least two of the following six criteria enumerated at 8 CFR 204.5(i)(3)(i):
162	
163	> 1\. Documentation of the beneficiary\'s receipt of major prizes or awards for outstanding achievement in the academic field;
164	>
165	> 2\. Documentation of the beneficiary\'s membership in associations in the academic field which require outstanding achievements of their members;
166	>
167	> 3\. Published material in professional publications written by others about the beneficiary\'s work in the academic field;
168	>
169	> 4\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s participation, either individually or on a panel, as the judge of the work of others in the same or an allied academic field;
170	>
171	> 5\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s original scientific or scholarly research contributions to the academic field;
172	>
173	> 6\. Evidence of the beneficiary\'s authorship of scholarly books or articles (in scholarly journals with international circulation) in the academic field.
174	
175	The beneficiary must also demonstrate a minimum of three years of experience in teaching or research in the academic field. This experience requirement is measured as of the date of filing and may include experience gained during graduate study, provided that the experience was in a teaching or research capacity. Post-doctoral research positions, visiting professorships, and comparable roles at research institutions all qualify toward this requirement.
176	
177	With respect to Dr. Katarina Breitner, her profile is well suited to the EB-1B classification. She holds fourteen published papers and three patents, has served as a journal peer reviewer, and has been employed as a Principal Researcher at Aethon Semiconductor GmbH in Munich since approximately March 2020 --- a period of nearly five years, which comfortably satisfies the three-year experience requirement. Dr. Breitner\'s qualifications may support criteria 4 (judging the work of others through peer review), 5 (original scientific research contributions, as evidenced by her patents and publications), and 6 (authorship of scholarly articles in journals with international circulation). Satisfying three of the six criteria exceeds the regulatory minimum of two, which strengthens the overall petition.
178	
179	**[4.3 EB-1B Employer/Petitioner Requirements]{.underline}**
180	
181	The petitioning employer must file Form I-140 on behalf of the beneficiary. The employer must offer the beneficiary a permanent research or teaching position in the United States. The position must be a tenured or tenure-track teaching position at a university or institution of higher education, or a comparable permanent research position at a university, institution of higher education, or private employer.
182	
183	The job offer must be bona fide, and the employer must demonstrate that the position is permanent in nature. A position that is temporary, project-based, or contingent upon external funding may not satisfy the EB-1B requirements. The offered position must be in the beneficiary\'s specific academic field --- that is, the academic discipline in which the beneficiary has been recognized as outstanding. For example, a beneficiary recognized as outstanding in applied physics must be offered a research or teaching position in applied physics or a closely related discipline, rather than an unrelated field.
184	
185	The employer\'s petition must include a letter describing the terms of the employment offer, including the title, duties, and permanence of the position. Supporting documentation should include organizational charts, departmental structure information, and descriptions of the research activities in which the beneficiary will be engaged. The employer should clearly articulate the connection between the offered position and the beneficiary\'s area of academic expertise.
186	
187	For Aethon\'s planned EB-1B petitions for research scientists, the employer should be prepared to demonstrate the nature and permanence of the research position offered. Aethon should document the research activities of its Austin facility, including the scope of ongoing projects in semiconductor design, process development, and photonics research, and should provide detailed position descriptions for each research scientist role. Letters from Aethon\'s Chief Technology Officer or Vice President of Research and Development confirming the permanent nature of the positions and the company\'s commitment to maintaining an active research program will be important supporting evidence.
188	
189	**[4.4 EB-1B Filing Information]{.underline}**
190	
191	The EB-1B petition is filed using Form I-140, Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers. The current base filing fee is \$700, and premium processing is available through Form I-907 for an additional fee of \$2,805. No labor certification through the PERM process is required. Unlike the EB-1A classification, the EB-1B category does not permit self-petitions; the qualifying employer must file the I-140 on the beneficiary\'s behalf. Processing timelines and priority date rules are consistent with those described in Section 3.4 for the EB-1A classification.
192	
193	**[Section 5: EB-2 --- Members of Professions Holding Advanced Degrees or Persons of Exceptional Ability]{.underline}**
194	
195	**[5.1 Overview and Statutory Basis]{.underline}**
196	
197	The EB-2 classification is the second preference employment-based immigrant visa category, established under INA § 203(b)(2) and governed by the regulations at 8 CFR 204.5(k). The EB-2 category encompasses two distinct sub-categories: (a) members of the professions holding advanced degrees, as defined under INA § 203(b)(2) and 8 CFR 204.5(k)(1); and (b) persons of exceptional ability in the sciences, arts, or business, as defined under INA § 203(b)(2) and 8 CFR 204.5(k)(2).
198	
199	The dual-path structure of the EB-2 category --- advanced degree professionals on the one hand, and individuals of exceptional ability on the other --- provides meaningful flexibility for petitioners and beneficiaries. A beneficiary need only qualify under one of the two sub-categories, not both. The advanced degree path focuses on the beneficiary\'s academic qualifications, while the exceptional ability path focuses on the beneficiary\'s demonstrated track record of achievement in the field. In many cases, a beneficiary may qualify under both sub-categories, and the petition may be framed accordingly.
200	
201	The EB-2 classification generally requires both a job offer from a U.S. employer and a labor certification through the PERM process (ETA Form 9089). However, an important exception exists: the National Interest Waiver (NIW), authorized under INA § 203(b)(2)(B), permits waiver of both the job offer requirement and the PERM labor certification requirement where the beneficiary\'s proposed endeavor is deemed to be in the national interest of the United States. The NIW is discussed in detail in Section 5.4 below.
202	
203	**[5.2 EB-2(a) --- Advanced Degree Professionals]{.underline}**
204	
205	Under the EB-2(a) sub-category, the term \"advanced degree\" is defined as any United States academic degree, or a foreign equivalent degree, above a bachelor\'s degree. This includes master\'s degrees, doctoral degrees, and professional degrees such as the J.D., M.D., or equivalent. Alternatively, a United States bachelor\'s degree (or foreign equivalent) combined with at least five years of progressive post-baccalaureate experience in the specialty may be considered the equivalent of an advanced degree for purposes of this classification.
206	
207	The advanced degree must be related to the position offered by the petitioning employer. A beneficiary holding a doctoral degree in electrical engineering, for example, would qualify for an EB-2(a) petition for a position as a senior design engineer or research scientist in semiconductor technology, provided the position requires an advanced degree in that field or a related discipline.
208	
209	The EB-2(a) sub-category requires PERM labor certification and a job offer from a U.S. employer, unless the beneficiary qualifies for a National Interest Waiver. The PERM process involves labor market testing to demonstrate that there are insufficient available, qualified, willing United States workers to fill the offered position at the prevailing wage.
210	
211	Most of Aethon\'s planned research scientist hires, with salary ranges of approximately \$150,000 to \$195,000, hold doctoral degrees and would qualify under the EB-2(a) sub-category. Dr. Katarina Breitner (PhD, Applied Physics, Technische Universität München, 2017) and Dr. Wei-Lin Chang (PhD, Electrical Engineering, National Taiwan University, 2019) both clearly qualify by virtue of their doctoral degrees. Rajeev Malhotra (MS, Computer Engineering, IIT Bombay, 2020) also qualifies for EB-2(a) classification by virtue of his master\'s degree, which constitutes an advanced degree above the bachelor\'s level.
212	
213	**[5.3 EB-2(b) --- Exceptional Ability]{.underline}**
214	
215	Under the EB-2(b) sub-category, \"exceptional ability\" is defined as a degree of expertise significantly above that ordinarily encountered in the sciences, arts, or business. This standard is lower than the \"extraordinary ability\" standard applicable to the EB-1A classification but still requires the beneficiary to demonstrate a level of achievement and recognition that places the beneficiary meaningfully above the typical professional in the field.
216	
217	To qualify for the EB-2(b) sub-category, the beneficiary must provide evidence satisfying at least three of the following six criteria under 8 CFR 204.5(k)(3)(ii):
218	
219	> 1\. An official academic record showing that the beneficiary has a degree, diploma, certificate, or similar award from an institution of learning relating to the area of exceptional ability;
220	>
221	> 2\. Letters from current or former employers documenting at least ten years of full-time experience in the occupation for which the beneficiary is being sought;
222	>
223	> 3\. A license to practice the profession or certification for a particular profession or occupation;
224	>
225	> 4\. Evidence that the beneficiary has commanded a salary or other remuneration for services which demonstrates exceptional ability;
226	>
227	> 5\. Membership in professional associations;
228	>
229	> 6\. Evidence of recognition for achievements and significant contributions to the industry or field by peers, governmental entities, or professional or business organizations.
230	
231	The regulations also permit the submission of comparable evidence if the six criteria listed above do not readily apply to the beneficiary\'s occupation. This comparable evidence provision provides additional flexibility for beneficiaries in specialized or non-traditional fields.
232	
233	The EB-2(b) sub-category requires PERM labor certification and a job offer from a U.S. employer, unless the beneficiary qualifies for a National Interest Waiver.
234	
235	**[5.4 EB-2 National Interest Waiver (NIW)]{.underline}**
236	
237	The National Interest Waiver (NIW) is an important exception to the standard EB-2 requirements. Under INA § 203(b)(2)(B), the Attorney General (now the Secretary of Homeland Security, through USCIS) may waive both the job offer requirement and the PERM labor certification requirement when doing so would be in the national interest of the United States. The NIW thus permits self-petitions: the beneficiary may file Form I-140 without an employer sponsor and without first obtaining labor certification.
238	
239	**The Dhanasar Framework.** The governing legal standard for NIW adjudication is set forth in *Matter of Dhanasar*, 26 I&N Dec. 884 (AAO 2016), which replaced the prior *Matter of New York State Department of Transportation* (NYSDOT) framework. Under the three-prong *Dhanasar* test, the petitioner must demonstrate:
240	
241	> **Prong 1:** The proposed endeavor has both substantial merit and national importance.
242	>
243	> **Prong 2:** The beneficiary is well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor.
244	
245	If the petitioner establishes both prongs, the NIW may be approved.
246	
247	**Prong 1 Analysis --- Substantial Merit and National Importance.** The concept of \"substantial merit\" encompasses a wide range of potential benefits, including economic, cultural, educational, scientific, technological, and other societal contributions. The petitioner must articulate a specific proposed endeavor and explain how that endeavor possesses substantial intrinsic merit. \"National importance\" does not require that the endeavor have a nationwide geographic scope. An endeavor that is local or regional in nature may still be of national importance if its implications extend beyond the specific locality or if it addresses issues of national concern. In the semiconductor industry, USCIS has recognized that areas such as advanced chip design, semiconductor process development, photonics research, quantum computing, and national security applications possess both substantial merit and national importance. The passage of the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 and the associated federal investment in domestic semiconductor manufacturing capacity further underscore the national importance of this field.
248	
249	**Prong 2 Analysis --- Well Positioned to Advance the Endeavor.** USCIS evaluates a range of factors in assessing whether the beneficiary is well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor, including the beneficiary\'s education, skills, knowledge, and record of success in related or similar efforts. Additional relevant factors include whether the beneficiary has developed a model or plan for future activity, the extent of progress already made toward achieving the proposed endeavor, and evidence of interest from potential customers, users, investors, or other relevant entities. For STEM professionals, patents, published research, citation records, industry recognition, and letters from experts in the field are strong indicators that the beneficiary is well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor. A detailed description of the beneficiary\'s planned research agenda or professional activities in the United States is advisable.
250	
251	**Practical Application for Aethon.** For Aethon\'s semiconductor research scientists and engineers, the NIW may be particularly viable given the national importance of domestic semiconductor manufacturing and design capabilities, especially in light of the CHIPS and Science Act. Dr. Breitner\'s work in advanced node process development and photonics research at Aethon Semiconductor GmbH (Munich) demonstrates the kind of cutting-edge work that supports prong 1. Her fourteen publications, three patents, and track record of independent research strongly support prong 2.
252	
253	The NIW is also a useful option for candidates like Rajeev Malhotra (Indian national, MS Computer Engineering, IIT Bombay, 2020), who is currently employed by Ridgeline Staffing Solutions, Inc. and has no prior Aethon employment. Because the NIW does not require current employment with the petitioning employer and permits self-petition, Mr. Malhotra can file an NIW-based I-140 independently while simultaneously pursuing direct employment with Aethon. This flexibility is particularly valuable for candidates who are not yet employed by the intended employer or who are in staffing arrangements that complicate traditional employer-sponsored petitions. Practitioners should be aware, however, that the India EB-2 visa backlog may result in significant wait times between I-140 approval and visa availability, which must be factored into the overall immigration strategy.
254	
255	**[5.5 EB-2 Filing Information]{.underline}**
256	
257	The EB-2 petition is filed using Form I-140, Immigrant Petition for Alien Workers. The current base filing fee for Form I-140 is \$700, and premium processing is available through Form I-907 for an additional fee of \$2,805. For the standard EB-2 pathway (with PERM), the employer must first obtain a labor certification by filing ETA Form 9089 with the Department of Labor. There is no government filing fee for the PERM application, but the associated legal costs for recruitment, advertising, and preparation of the PERM application typically range from \$5,000 to \$10,000. The PERM process currently takes approximately eight to eighteen months, and the I-140 cannot be filed until the PERM application has been certified.
258	
259	For EB-2/NIW self-petitions, the I-140 is filed directly with USCIS without a PERM application, which eliminates both the PERM processing time and the associated legal costs. The priority date for an EB-2 petition is established upon the filing of the I-140 (or upon the filing of the PERM application, if PERM is required, provided the PERM is ultimately certified and the I-140 is approved).
260	
261	As a budget consideration for Aethon, with an average per-petition immigration budget of approximately \$34,285.71 (based on a total immigration budget of \$1,200,000 for thirty-five planned hires), EB-2/NIW self-petitions represent a cost-effective path because they avoid the PERM process and its associated costs. All categories covered in this document fall within the per-petition budget when accounting for attorney fees and government filing fees.
262	
263	**[Section 6: Comparative Analysis and Category Selection Guidance]{.underline}**
264	
265	**[6.1 O-1A vs. EB-1A]{.underline}**
266	
267	The O-1A nonimmigrant classification and the EB-1A immigrant classification both target individuals of extraordinary ability, but they serve fundamentally different purposes and confer different immigration benefits. The O-1A is a temporary (nonimmigrant) visa classification that authorizes employment in the United States for a defined period, while the EB-1A is an immigrant (permanent residence) classification that leads to a green card.
268	
269	The O-1A evidentiary criteria track closely to the EB-1A criteria, as both are designed to identify individuals who have reached the top of their respective fields in the sciences, business, education, or athletics. Many of the same types of evidence --- awards, publications, original contributions, judging, high salary, leading roles --- are relevant to both classifications. However, the EB-1A classification generally carries a higher evidentiary burden in practice, as it requires a showing of \"sustained national or international acclaim\" and the two-step analysis under *Kazarian*, whereas the O-1A focuses on whether the beneficiary is among a \"small percentage who have risen to the very top of the field.\"
270	
271	A strategic approach for Aethon\'s candidates is to file an O-1A petition first and, upon approval, use the approved O-1A petition as supporting evidence for a subsequent EB-1A immigrant petition. An O-1A approval, while not binding on the adjudicator reviewing the EB-1A petition, serves as a strong indicator that the beneficiary has been previously recognized as meeting an extraordinary ability standard. This sequential approach also allows the beneficiary to commence employment in the United States in O-1A status while the longer-term immigrant visa process unfolds.
272	
273	One important procedural distinction: the O-1A requires an employer petition, while the EB-1A permits self-petition. This provides additional strategic flexibility in the immigrant visa context, particularly for beneficiaries who may change employers or who wish to maintain control over their own immigration process.
274	
275	**[6.2 EB-1A vs. EB-1B vs. EB-2/NIW]{.underline}**
276	
277	The three primary immigrant visa categories for highly qualified professionals --- EB-1A, EB-1B, and EB-2/NIW --- differ significantly in their standards, requirements, and strategic implications. The following comparison summarizes the key distinctions:
278	
279	The EB-1A classification carries the highest evidentiary standard (extraordinary ability demonstrated by sustained national or international acclaim), does not require an employer sponsor, and does not require PERM labor certification. The EB-1B classification applies an intermediate standard (international recognition as outstanding in a specific academic field), requires an employer sponsor, and does not require PERM labor certification, but the employer must offer a qualifying permanent research or teaching position. The EB-2/NIW classification applies a lower standard (advanced degree or exceptional ability, combined with the *Dhanasar* national interest test), permits self-petition, and does not require PERM labor certification.
280	
281	For Aethon\'s research scientists, we recommend considering EB-1B as a primary path, given that these candidates typically hold doctoral degrees, have substantial publication and research records, and can satisfy the EB-1B evidentiary criteria with relative ease. The EB-2/NIW should be pursued as a concurrent or backup strategy. For Aethon\'s engineers who may not meet the EB-1B academic field requirements, the EB-2/NIW or EB-1A (if qualifications are sufficiently strong) are the recommended paths.
282	
283	Where a beneficiary\'s priority date is current at the time of filing, Form I-485 (Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status) may be filed concurrently with the Form I-140, which can significantly reduce the overall timeline to permanent residence.
284

43	**II.A. Overview of TN Status**
44	
45	TN nonimmigrant status is authorized under Chapter 16 of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) effective July 1, 2020, while preserving the TN provisions formerly found in NAFTA Chapter 16. TN status is implemented in domestic law through Section 214(e) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) and the corresponding regulations at 8 CFR 214.6.
46	
47	TN status is available exclusively to citizens of Canada and Mexico. It permits the temporary entry of qualifying professionals to engage in prearranged business activities at a professional level for a U.S. employer. The classification is designed to facilitate the cross-border movement of professionals in designated occupations, consistent with the trade liberalization objectives of the USMCA.
48	
49	TN is a nonimmigrant classification. For Canadian citizens, TN status does not require the filing of a USCIS petition; Canadian nationals may apply directly at a U.S. port of entry or preclearance facility by presenting the requisite documentation. Mexican citizens, by contrast, must obtain a TN visa at a U.S. consulate abroad or, if present in the United States in a valid immigration status, may apply for a change of status or extension of status through the filing of Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, with USCIS.
50	
51	With respect to Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc., the TN classification may be applicable to certain Canadian or Mexican national candidates among the planned 35 foreign national hires scheduled across Q3 2025 through Q4 2026. It should be noted that the three representative candidates currently under evaluation --- Dr. Wei-Lin Chang (Taiwanese national), Dr. Katarina Breitner (German national), and Rajeev Malhotra (Indian national) --- are not TN-eligible due to their nationalities. Nevertheless, the TN category should be included in the comprehensive eligibility matrix for completeness, as Aethon\'s expansion plan encompasses multiple visa categories and future Canadian or Mexican candidates may emerge during the hiring process.
52	
53	**II.B. Eligible Professions and Qualifying Criteria**
54	
55	TN status is limited to professions listed in Appendix 2 of the USMCA (commonly referred to as the \"USMCA Professions List\"). This appendix enumerates approximately 63 professional categories for which TN admission is available. The list is specific and exhaustive; professions not included on the list are not eligible for TN classification regardless of the applicant\'s qualifications.
56	
57	Among the professional categories on the USMCA Professions List, the following are most relevant to Aethon Semiconductor Technologies\' anticipated hiring needs in semiconductor design, firmware/software engineering, and related research disciplines:
58	
59	> • **Engineer:** The USMCA Professions List requires a baccalaureate degree or licenciatura degree for the Engineer category. This encompasses a broad range of engineering specializations, including electrical engineering, computer engineering, and related fields directly applicable to semiconductor design and fabrication support.
60	>
61	> • **Computer Systems Analyst:** This category requires a baccalaureate degree or licenciatura degree, or alternatively, a post-secondary diploma or post-secondary certificate and three years of experience. Computer Systems Analysts who perform work involving the analysis and design of computer-based systems may qualify under this designation, though practitioners should exercise care to ensure the position duties align with the specific occupational description rather than overlapping with software development roles not encompassed by the category.
62	>
63	> • **Scientist:** The Scientist category requires a baccalaureate degree or licenciatura degree. Research scientists engaged in semiconductor physics, photonics research, or advanced node process development may qualify under this designation, provided the position genuinely requires the individual to function in a professional scientific capacity.
64	
65	To qualify for TN status, several conditions must be met. First, the position offered by the U.S. employer must require the professional to perform services in one of the listed professions. The job duties must correspond to the professional activities typically associated with the designated occupation. Second, the beneficiary must possess the credentials specified for that profession in the USMCA Professions List, which typically consists of a bachelor\'s degree or its equivalent in the relevant field, though certain categories accept alternative credential combinations. Third, there must be a prearranged full-time or part-time professional position with a U.S. employer; the arrangement must be in place prior to the TN application or admission. Fourth, the beneficiary must meet all applicable state and federal licensing requirements if the profession is regulated in the state of intended employment.
66	
67	Notably, TN status does not require the filing of a labor condition application (LCA) with the Department of Labor, unlike H-1B status. There is also no annual numerical cap on TN admissions, which provides a significant procedural advantage relative to the H-1B category.
68	
69	**II.C. Duration of Status and Extensions**
70	
71	TN status is granted for an initial period of up to three years per admission, as provided under 8 CFR 214.6(h). This three-year period has been in effect since the regulatory amendment that took effect in 2008, replacing the prior one-year admission period that had applied under the original NAFTA-era regulations. The current three-year admission period remains in effect and applies to both Canadian and Mexican TN professionals.
72	
73	Extensions of stay in TN status may be granted in increments of up to three years per extension. There is no maximum cumulative limit on the number of extensions that may be obtained, and consequently no statutory ceiling on the total duration of time an individual may remain in TN status. A TN professional may, in theory, remain in TN status indefinitely through successive three-year extensions.
74	
75	However, practitioners should be aware that prolonged TN status may raise questions regarding the beneficiary\'s nonimmigrant intent. Because TN is a nonimmigrant classification that does not permit dual intent, an individual who has remained in TN status for an extended period --- particularly one who has filed or is the beneficiary of an immigrant visa petition --- may face heightened scrutiny at the time of extension or readmission. Practitioners should counsel TN candidates on the importance of maintaining credible nonimmigrant intent documentation, including evidence of ties to the home country and the temporary nature of the U.S. assignment.
76	
77	Dependents of TN professionals --- specifically, spouses and unmarried children under the age of 21 --- may accompany the principal TN holder in TD (Trade Dependent) status. TD dependents are admitted for the same validity period as the principal\'s TN status. TD dependents may not engage in employment in the United States but are permitted to pursue educational activities, including enrollment in academic programs on a full-time or part-time basis.
78	
79	**II.D. Compensation Requirements**
80	
81	TN visa holders must be compensated at a level consistent with the professional nature of the position for which they are admitted. The compensation offered should reflect the professional qualifications required for the position and be commensurate with the prevailing standards for similarly situated professionals in the relevant occupational field and geographic area.
82	
83	Consistent with USCIS guidance, TN professionals are subject to a minimum prevailing wage requirement equivalent to the H-1B prevailing wage standards. USCIS has indicated that TN professionals should be compensated at no less than the applicable prevailing wage for the occupation and geographic area, and in no event below a minimum salary of \$60,000 for professional positions. This threshold ensures that TN professionals are not admitted at compensation levels that would undercut the domestic labor market for similarly qualified U.S. workers in the same occupational classification. (See USCIS Policy Manual, Vol. 2, Part L; cf. H-1B prevailing wage methodology under 20 CFR 655.731.)
84	
85	The prevailing wage obligation for TN professionals operates in a manner substantially similar to the H-1B prevailing wage framework administered by the Department of Labor. Petitioners and employers should ensure that the offered salary meets or exceeds the applicable wage level for the Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code and metropolitan statistical area in which the TN professional will be employed. The four-tier wage level system (Level I through Level IV) applies, with the specific level determined by reference to the complexity of the position, the degree of supervision required, and the experience and education of the beneficiary relative to the occupation.
86	
87	\> **Practice Tip:** For Aethon\'s planned hires, the salary ranges under consideration --- hardware engineers \$135,000--\$175,000; software engineers \$140,000--\$185,000; research scientists \$150,000--\$195,000; managerial positions \$190,000--\$240,000 --- would comfortably exceed the \$60,000 minimum threshold described above. Nevertheless, practitioners should confirm prevailing wage compliance for each individual position by obtaining a prevailing wage determination from the National Prevailing Wage Center (NPWC) or, at minimum, by referencing the applicable Online Wage Library (OWL) data for the Austin-Round Rock, TX metropolitan statistical area. Failure to meet the prevailing wage for the specific SOC code and wage level applicable to each position could result in compliance issues and potential petition challenges.
88	
89	Employers should maintain documentation of the compensation offered to each TN professional and retain records demonstrating that the salary offered meets or exceeds the applicable prevailing wage standard. Such documentation should be maintained in the employer\'s public access files or equivalent internal records for the duration of the TN professional\'s employment.
90	
91	**II.E. Filing Procedures and Fees**
92	
93	The filing procedures for TN status differ depending on whether the applicant is a Canadian citizen or a Mexican citizen.
94	
95	**Canadian Citizens.** Canadian nationals may apply directly for TN status at a U.S. port of entry or preclearance facility. The applicant must present the following documentation at the time of application: (1) a letter from the prospective U.S. employer describing the professional position, the anticipated duration of the assignment, and the compensation to be provided; (2) proof of Canadian citizenship (e.g., a valid Canadian passport or birth certificate combined with government-issued photo identification); and (3) proof of professional credentials, including educational degrees, transcripts, professional licenses, and any other documentation establishing that the applicant possesses the qualifications specified in the USMCA Professions List for the applicable profession. The Canadian applicant must also pay the applicable I-94 fee at the time of admission. No Form I-129 petition is required for the initial admission of a Canadian TN professional.
96	
97	**Mexican Citizens.** Mexican nationals must either file a Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, with USCIS (if applying for a change of status or extension from within the United States), or obtain a TN visa at a U.S. consulate abroad prior to seeking admission. The Form I-129 petition must be accompanied by the applicable base filing fee and all required supporting documentation.
98	
99	**Extensions and Amendments.** Extensions of TN status and amendments to existing TN employment (such as a change of employer) are filed on Form I-129 for both Canadian and Mexican nationals, if the application is made from within the United States. Canadian nationals who depart the United States may seek readmission in TN status at the border without filing Form I-129, provided they present updated documentation from the new or continuing employer.
100	
101	**Premium Processing.** Premium processing through the filing of Form I-907, Request for Premium Processing Service, is available for I-129-based TN petitions. Premium processing provides a 15-business-day adjudication timeline for an additional fee.
102	
103	**Fees Not Applicable to TN.** Unlike H-1B petitions, TN filings do not require payment of the ACWIA training fee, the fraud prevention and detection fee, or the Asylum Program fee. These fees are specific to H-1B and certain other nonimmigrant and employment-based categories and do not apply to the TN classification.
104	
105	The current I-129 base filing fee for electronic filing is \$780, effective April 1, 2024, as established in the USCIS fee schedule revision finalized in connection with the H-1B modernization final rule. This updated fee applies across all I-129 petition categories, including TN petitions filed by or on behalf of Mexican nationals and TN extension petitions filed on behalf of both Canadian and Mexican nationals.
106	
107	**II.F. Key Limitations and Considerations**
108	
109	Practitioners and clients should be mindful of several important limitations inherent in the TN classification:
110	
111	**No Dual Intent.** TN status does not permit dual intent. Unlike H-1B and L-1 classifications, TN beneficiaries must maintain credible nonimmigrant intent throughout their period of admission. This limitation can complicate transitions from TN status to employment-based immigrant visa processing (e.g., EB-2, EB-3 categories), as the filing of an immigrant visa petition or labor certification application (PERM) by the beneficiary\'s employer may be viewed as evidence of immigrant intent inconsistent with TN status. Practitioners should carefully sequence any immigrant visa strategy for current TN holders.
112	
113	**No Self-Employment.** TN professionals must work for a U.S. employer and may not be self-employed. The employment relationship must involve an employer-employee relationship in which the U.S. employer exercises control and direction over the TN professional\'s work.
114	
115	**Position Must Fall Within Listed Profession.** The position offered must fall squarely within one of the professions enumerated in the USMCA Professions List. Positions that represent \"catch-all\" or hybrid roles combining professional and non-professional duties may be challenged by USCIS or CBP officers at the port of entry. Practitioners should ensure that the job description clearly maps to a single listed profession.
116	
117	**No Portability.** There is no portability provision for TN status analogous to the H-1B portability provisions under the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21) § 105. A TN professional must obtain new TN authorization --- whether through a new I-129 petition, a new visa stamp, or new admission at the port of entry --- before beginning work for a new employer. Unauthorized employment with a new employer prior to obtaining new TN authorization may result in a violation of status.
118	
119	**Nationality Requirement.** TN status is available only to citizens of Canada and Mexico. Permanent residents of these countries who hold citizenship of a third country are not eligible. This limitation is strictly construed.
120	
121	**[III. H-1B Cap-Exempt Employer --- Expanded Definition]{.underline}**
122	
123	**III.A. Background.** Under INA § 214(g)(5), certain employers are exempt from the annual H-1B numerical cap. The regular annual cap is set at 65,000 H-1B visas per fiscal year, with an additional 20,000 visas available under the U.S. advanced degree exemption (commonly known as the \"master\'s cap\"), for a combined total of 85,000 cap-subject visas per fiscal year. Demand for H-1B classification routinely exceeds this annual allotment, making the cap-exemption analysis a critical component of immigration strategy for employers that may qualify.
124	
125	Historically, cap-exempt employers were identified in the statute and regulations as falling within a defined set of institutional categories. The statutory framework at INA § 214(g)(5)(A)--(B) and the implementing regulations identified the following categories of employers whose H-1B petitions are not counted against the annual cap: (1) institutions of higher education as defined in section 101(a) of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (20 U.S.C. § 1001(a)); (2) nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with such institutions; (3) nonprofit research organizations; and (4) governmental research organizations.
126	
127	In practice, however, the second category --- \"nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with institutions of higher education\" --- was not always clearly delineated in USCIS adjudicatory guidance or in some practitioner resources. The firm\'s H-1B Regulatory Summary currently lists only \"institutions of higher education, nonprofit research organizations, and governmental research organizations\" as cap-exempt employers, and does not separately enumerate the \"nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with\" category. This omission should be corrected, as discussed below.
128	
129	**III.B. H-1B Modernization Rule --- Expanded Cap-Exempt Definition**
130	
131	The H-1B modernization final rule, published in January 2024 with provisions taking effect on various dates through early 2025, codified and clarified the expanded definition of cap-exempt employers under the H-1B program. Among the most significant clarifications in the modernization rule is the explicit articulation of the four distinct categories of employers whose petitions are exempt from the annual H-1B numerical cap.
132	
133	The updated rule, as reflected in the amended regulatory text at 8 CFR 214.2(h)(8)(ii)(B), explicitly adds and clarifies the category of \"nonprofit entities or governmental research organizations that are related to or affiliated with institutions of higher education.\" Under the amended regulation, a nonprofit entity qualifies for the cap exemption if it is \"related to or affiliated with\" an institution of higher education, meaning that it is connected or associated with such an institution through shared ownership or control, or through a formal written affiliation agreement that establishes an institutional relationship between the nonprofit entity and the qualifying institution of higher education.
134	
135	The expanded definition now encompasses four categories of cap-exempt employers:
136	
137	1\. **Institutions of higher education** as defined in 20 U.S.C. § 1001(a);
138	
139	2\. **Nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with an institution of higher education**, where the relationship is demonstrated through shared ownership or control or a formal written affiliation agreement;
140	
141	3\. **Nonprofit research organizations**; and
142	
143	4\. **Governmental research organizations.**
144	
145	Practitioners should be aware that the firm\'s current H-1B Regulatory Summary references only three categories (institutions of higher education, nonprofit research organizations, and governmental research organizations) and does not separately enumerate the \"nonprofit entities related to or affiliated with\" category. The H-1B Regulatory Summary should be updated to reflect this expanded and clarified four-category definition to ensure consistency across the firm\'s guidance documents and accuracy in client counseling.
146	
147	The modernization rule also clarified the circumstances under which cap-exempt status may apply in concurrent or sequential employment arrangements. Under the updated provisions, an H-1B beneficiary whose worksite is at a cap-exempt entity may qualify for cap exemption even if the petitioning employer is itself cap-subject, provided that the beneficiary\'s work is performed primarily at or for the benefit of the cap-exempt institution. This analysis is particularly relevant in scenarios involving collaborative research arrangements, sponsored research agreements, and joint academic-industry programs where a for-profit employer\'s employees may be stationed at or working substantially with university research laboratories.
148	
149	With respect to Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, Inc., the company is a for-profit Delaware corporation and does not itself qualify as a cap-exempt employer. However, if Aethon engineers or research scientists are placed at or collaborate substantially with a university research lab --- for example, under a sponsored research agreement with a qualifying institution of higher education --- the cap-exemption analysis may apply to specific petitions filed on behalf of those individuals. This consideration is particularly relevant to Aethon\'s five planned research scientist hires, who may be engaged in collaborative projects with university partners. The firm should proactively assess whether any existing or planned university research partnerships could support cap-exempt H-1B filings for specific candidates.
150	
151	**III.C. Cap-Exempt Petition Procedures**
152	
153	H-1B petitions filed by or on behalf of cap-exempt employers may be filed at any time during the fiscal year and are not subject to the H-1B registration period or the annual lottery selection process. This provides a significant procedural advantage, as cap-exempt petitioners are not dependent on lottery selection and can time their filings according to business needs and the beneficiary\'s availability.
154	
155	The petitioning employer bears the burden of demonstrating that it qualifies as a cap-exempt entity, or that the beneficiary\'s employment qualifies for cap exemption based on the worksite or nature of the work being performed. USCIS may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) seeking documentation of the qualifying relationship between the petitioner and a cap-exempt institution, particularly in cases involving the \"related to or affiliated with\" category, where the nature and extent of the affiliation must be established through written agreements, organizational documents, or other evidence of the institutional relationship.
156	
157	It is important to note that cap-exempt status attaches to the petition, not to the beneficiary in perpetuity. If a beneficiary who was previously counted as cap-exempt subsequently seeks to change employers and the new employer is cap-subject, the beneficiary may need to be counted against the annual H-1B cap unless the beneficiary has previously been counted against the cap --- that is, unless the beneficiary previously held H-1B status under a cap-subject petition during the same six-year period. Practitioners should carefully analyze each beneficiary\'s H-1B history when advising on employer changes to determine whether recapture of a cap number is necessary.

245	**V.A. O-1 Policy Manual Revisions (2023--2024)**
246	
247	USCIS issued significant updates to its Policy Manual in 2023 regarding the adjudication of O-1 visa petitions. These updates, reflected in Volume 2, Part M of the USCIS Policy Manual, clarified the evidentiary standards applicable to both O-1A (extraordinary ability in the sciences, business, education, or athletics) and O-1B (extraordinary ability or achievement in the arts, or extraordinary achievement in the motion picture or television industry) petitions.
248	
249	The updated guidance emphasizes a two-step analytical framework for O-1 adjudications:
250	
251	1\. **Step One --- Regulatory Criteria Analysis:** The adjudicator must determine whether the evidence submitted meets the plain language of at least three of the applicable regulatory criteria. For O-1A petitions, these criteria are set forth at 8 CFR 214.2(o)(3)(iii) and include, among others, documentation of awards, published material about the beneficiary, original contributions of major significance, and authorship of scholarly articles. For O-1B petitions, the criteria are set forth at 8 CFR 214.2(o)(3)(iv) and are tailored to artistic achievement.
252	
253	2\. **Step Two --- Final Merits Determination:** Having determined that the evidence satisfies at least three criteria, the adjudicator must conduct a final merits determination evaluating the totality of the evidence to determine whether the beneficiary has attained and sustained national or international acclaim in the relevant field.
254	
255	It is important to note that the O-1A criteria under 8 CFR 214.2(o)(3)(iii) are distinct from the O-1B criteria under 8 CFR 214.2(o)(3)(iv). The O-1A criteria closely track the EB-1A extraordinary ability factors used in employment-based first preference immigrant visa adjudications. The O-1B criteria, by contrast, are specifically tailored to the arts and entertainment industries and involve different evidentiary considerations.
256	
257	For Aethon\'s purposes, engineers and research scientists would be evaluated under the O-1A (sciences) standard, not the O-1B (arts) standard. The firm\'s separate Employment-Based Immigrant & Nonimmigrant Extraordinary Ability Categories guidance document should be consulted for the specific criteria applicable to each O-1 sub-category and the corresponding EB-1 immigrant visa classifications. Aethon currently has 2 employees in O-1B status, as reflected in the company\'s current immigration portfolio.

259	**V.B. EB-2/NIW Guidance Updates**
260	
261	USCIS guidance continues to apply the three-prong analytical framework established in *Matter of Dhanasar*, 26 I&N Dec. 884 (AAO 2016), for the adjudication of National Interest Waiver (NIW) petitions under the EB-2 employment-based second preference immigrant visa category. The *Dhanasar* framework replaced the prior *Matter of New York State Department of Transportation* (NYSDOT) standard and established a more flexible test for evaluating NIW eligibility.
262	
263	Under *Dhanasar*, a petitioner seeking a National Interest Waiver must demonstrate that:
264	
265	1\. The proposed endeavor has both substantial merit and national importance;
266	
267	2\. The beneficiary is well positioned to advance the proposed endeavor; and
268	
269	3\. On balance, it would be beneficial to the United States to waive the requirements of a job offer and thus of a labor certification.
270	
271	The USCIS Policy Manual (Vol. 6, Part F, Chapter 5) incorporates the *Dhanasar* framework and provides illustrative examples of how each prong may be satisfied across various fields of endeavor. Adjudicators are instructed to evaluate each prong independently and to consider the totality of the evidence presented in support of the petition.
272	
273	With respect to Aethon Semiconductor Technologies, semiconductor design and advanced chip research may constitute endeavors of substantial merit and national importance, particularly in light of the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-167) and the related federal emphasis on expanding domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research capacity. The national importance prong may be strengthened by evidence demonstrating the connection between the beneficiary\'s proposed work and the national strategic interest in semiconductor supply chain resilience and technological leadership. Practitioners evaluating EB-2/NIW strategies for Aethon\'s research scientist candidates should cross-reference the firm\'s Employment-Based Immigrant & Nonimmigrant Extraordinary Ability Categories guidance document for a comprehensive discussion of the EB-2/NIW criteria and evidentiary requirements.

275	**V.C. Prevailing Wage Updates**
276	
277	The Department of Labor (DOL) prevailing wage determination process continues to be a required element of the H-1B petition process. Under 20 CFR 655.731, employers filing H-1B petitions must obtain a certified Labor Condition Application (LCA), which requires, among other attestations, that the employer will pay the H-1B worker at least the applicable prevailing wage for the occupation in the area of intended employment. Prevailing wage determinations are also required for H-1B1 (Chile/Singapore Free Trade Agreement professionals) and E-3 (Australian specialty occupation workers) petitions, which follow a similar wage attestation framework.
278	
279	The four prevailing wage levels (Level I through Level IV) established by the DOL remain in effect. The wage levels correspond to increasing levels of experience, education, supervisory responsibility, and special skills, with Level I representing entry-level positions and Level IV representing positions requiring the highest level of expertise. Employers must select the appropriate wage level based on the specific job requirements and the complexity of the duties to be performed, as described in the position\'s Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code.
